info.name: Jidoka
info.description:
Try Jidoka end to end: inject a task, watch AI triage discover a task type, onboard that type by describing how it should be handled, activate the generated pipeline, and see the waiting task get processed.

Start the server first:

    export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
    export JIDOKA_SAMPLE_DIR=./samples
    bun run dev

Run the requests in order. Each one stores the ids the next request needs in collection variables (taskId, typeId, pipelineId), so you can just keep clicking Send.

request.description:
Stores the task and immediately runs AI triage on it.

Responses:
- 201 with the triaged task
- 400 if title is missing
- 409 if sourceId + externalId already exist
- 502 if the model call failed (the task is still stored, and the body carries both `task` and `error`)

The first task in an empty system has no type to match, so triage proposes a new type and the task lands in `needs_onboarding`.

A task of a clearly different kind. Triage either proposes a second type, matches the first one, or — if it finds both plausible — parks the task in `needs_type_confirmation` with `typeCandidates` filled in.

Every task, newest first. This is exactly what the kanban board renders.

States: ingested, needs_type_confirmation, needs_onboarding, processing, assigned_ai, assigned_human, done, failed.

If any task is waiting on a type answer, its id is stored in {{taskId}} for the next folder.

The type registry that triage classifies against. Each type carries its name, description, example tasks, status (proposed / active), its active pipeline id, and every pipeline version built for it.

Stores the first type in {{typeId}} and the second in {{otherTypeId}}.

Use this for a task sitting in `needs_type_confirmation`. The task's title is saved as an example on the chosen type, so triage classifies better next time, and the task continues: it runs the type's pipeline, or waits for onboarding if there isn't one.
The description is what triage reads, so editing it changes how future tasks are classified.

Folds {{otherTypeId}} into {{typeId}}: its tasks are repointed and the duplicate type is deleted. Returns { "merged": true }.

Skip this request unless triage actually produced two near-duplicate types.

item.name: Build a pipeline from a description

exec: pm.test('a draft pipeline was built', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.eql(200));

request.description:
An AI agent turns your plain-language description into a pipeline definition and saves it as a DRAFT (nothing runs yet). The response body contains the full definition — read it before activating.

Steps it can emit: `ai` (one prompt), `agent` (loops over MCP tools until done), `mcp_tool` (one known call), `branch` (on an earlier step's output), `assign` (ai or human), `call_pipeline`.

It refuses definitions that use tools you don't have or that can end without assigning the task. 502 means the model failed twice.

Note: `agent` and `mcp_tool` steps only appear if MCP servers are configured via JIDOKA_MCP_SERVERS.
The stored definition, version and status (draft / active / superseded).

exec: console.log('now fetch GET /api/tasks — tasks of this type have been processed');

request.description:
Publishes the draft, marks the type active, and immediately runs it over every task of that type still sitting in `needs_onboarding`. Any previously active version becomes `superseded`.

After this, GET /api/tasks shows those tasks in assigned_ai / assigned_human, with the pipeline's output in `context` and its step log in `context.pipelineLog`.
The escape hatch: hand this task to a human as-is, without building a pipeline. The type stays `proposed`, so you can onboard it later.

item.name: Inject another task of the same kind

request.description: The payoff: this one is triaged into the existing type and its pipeline runs end to end with no interaction. The response shows the final state, the assignee the pipeline chose, and everything the steps wrote into `context`.
Confirm the board: processed tasks carry `assignee`, `context` (step outputs) and `context.pipelineLog` (which steps ran). A task in `failed` has `context.error`.
